title: 6DoF Motion Simulator
kind: Mechanical design, controls and FEA · December 2024 to now
alt: My sim rig from the side: the aluminum-extrusion cockpit, curved monitor, Moza wheel and Sparco seat
short: A motion platform for my sim rig, from FEA and kinematics to a full-scale test model.
text: The biggest thing I have built. I wanted my racing simulator to actually move, so I started designing a motion platform under it. The first layout was a pentapod with bent connecting rods. When a quote came back at $114 per rod, I redesigned it as a compact hexapod with straight members.

Along the way I ran FEA on the arms and frame, worked out the inverse kinematics and motor torque math in my own design workbook, wired the drives and power distribution, and built a full-scale model with printed gearboxes to debug homing, direction and geometry before buying final parts. The aluminum-extrusion cockpit is assembled, and I am now moving toward a more compact three-axis platform.

title: Aqua Guardian
kind: Team project with the Atholton Electronics Club · 2025 to now
alt: The orange Aqua Guardian buoy floating on Lake Elkhorn with fall trees behind it
short: A solar water-quality buoy, now floating in Lake Elkhorn. I lead the mechanical team.
text: Our Electronics Club’s floating water-quality station: it runs on solar power, samples the water it sits in, and uploads what it measures so anyone can check it. I co-founded the club and lead its mechanical team, so the hull, mounts, panels and enclosure are mine to figure out with the team. The steep A-frame solar panels keep it powered as it turns on its anchor. A foam ring at the waterline keeps it upright in wind. A teammate learning heat simulations caught that my antenna mount was hurting the signal, and we redesigned it together. We tested it through the ice in February and made the Samsung Solve for Tomorrow national semifinals as one of two Maryland teams (winning $10,000 for our school).

On November 11, 2026 we launched it in Lake Elkhorn. A Columbia Association crew took me out on their boat to set it down, and it has been uploading data ever since. It wasn’t a calm first day: the buoy went silent for hours after the crew left, and later the live data card told me there was a leak inside. Both turned out fine. The next job is calibrating five of the sensors.

title: 3D-Printed PC Case
alt: The printed orange and white case shell on my bench with the motherboard mounted inside
short: A gaming PC in a case I designed and printed, from a thin console to the smallest box I can manage.
text: I wanted a gaming PC that didn’t look like a PC, so I designed an ultra-thin, console-style case in Fusion 360 and printed it in pieces: orange front shells, white rear shells, black lids, and heat-set inserts everywhere. It can lie flat or stand up, and every plug comes out the back. It took twelve versions, a riser cable, and more reprints than I’d like to admit.

Then I tried to fit my main PC into the same shape, with a full ATX board and an RTX 3080, and the console idea stopped making sense. So I started over with one goal: the smallest volume those parts can fit in, smaller than the MODCASE Hyper that inspired it. I also used Claude to help with the CAD, which taught me a lot about where a tool like that helps and where it doesn’t. The full story is in the build journal.

title: Sim Racing Dash
kind: Raspberry Pi, Linux and 3D printing · 2025 to 2026
alt: The printed dash case with its 3.5-inch screen lit up
short: A $100 dashboard rebuilt from a spare Raspberry Pi and a printed case.
text: I needed a dashboard in front of me for RPMs, and the ones online cost $100 or more. I had a Raspberry Pi 3B+ and a small touchscreen lying around, so I designed a case that mounts to my Moza wheel base and posted it on Thingiverse.

Getting the software right took longer than the case. After a white screen I could not SSH into and Chromium refusing to open in kiosk mode, I rebuilt it on Pi OS Lite. Now it boots, joins Wi-Fi and opens a SimHub dashboard from my PC on its own. I wrote the whole setup down as a guide.

title: Go-Kart Restoration
alt: The Yamaha KT100 go-kart before the restoration
short: Bringing a Yamaha KT100 kart back to life, one problem at a time.
text: A Yamaha KT100 Swiss Hutless kart that had sat for years. It would only run for four seconds on starter fluid. Taking the carburetor apart, my dad and I found a worn pump diaphragm that would not pulse.

After that came a homemade kill switch (the factory harness was missing, and the kart nearly went through the garage door), a smaller split sprocket so it would not drag on the asphalt, a rusted axle, and yellow Dark Knight stripes. Then, finally, the first real drive.

title: Seatbelt Tensioner
alt: The racing harness installed on my sim rig seat
short: Motors that pull the harness tight under braking, driven by game data.
text: Motors behind the seat wind the harness straps tighter as the car brakes, using telemetry from the game through SimHub. I designed the housings, a 3:1 reduction and a center buckle, and wrote the control code.

The first version burned out its drivers a few minutes into a session, with smoke coming out of the controller box. I rebuilt the drive side and soldered my own power board to carry the current the motors actually pull.

title: DIY Handbrake
alt: My homemade handbrake lever mounted beside the seat
short: A homemade handbrake read by the game as an analog axis.
text: A handbrake for the rig built around a potentiometer and a Circuit Playground Express running CircuitPython. The game reads it as an analog axis, so I can pull it partway instead of just on or off.

title: AnTrust Variance Metrics
alt: The overview screen of the Variance Metrics tool
short: A tool for comparing board measurements, built during my internship.
text: An analysis and reporting tool I built during my metrology internship at AnTrust. It brings imported board readings, feature selection, comparisons and report export into one place, and handles failed readings, small samples and units honestly so a chart does not say more than the data does.

title: Mallet-Finger Splint
alt: A printed finger splint with ventilation holes
short: Custom splints for my dad, revised from his feedback.
text: After my dad hurt his finger, the splint he was given was uncomfortable to wear all day. I designed my own in CAD and printed revision after revision around what he told me: how it fit, whether he could type, how it felt by the evening. Each version on the journal shows what changed and why.

title: Enphase Solar Data Software
alt: My solar data dashboard on a monitor at the Maker Faire
short: Turning our household solar data into something you can explore.
text: Python and hvPlot tools for exploring the solar production data from our house: daily curves, monthly totals and the effect of weather. I showed it at the Columbia Maker Faire.
